name: Vera Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. We keep your answers confidential. Tell me what an ordinary working day looks like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am Vera Quinn, 58, and I help fit handrails and trim at a community hall rebuild. I left school early and came into this trade late, so the senior carpenter still shows me how to work around crooked stairs. I enjoy getting the line right, though my knees dislike ladders and I worry when a site is nearly finished.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because our four months of savings cannot carry us to retirement if robots take fitting work in 2031. Paid supervised training, honest job dates and a clear way to claim support if displaced would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the apprentices and older learners whether the paid practice hours really happen. If everyone is offered a course but nobody gets time on a staircase, the offer is paper.

headlineQuote: If everyone is offered a course but nobody gets time on a staircase, the offer is paper.
portrait: Vera is a **58-year-old junior** construction worker learning handrails and trim at a community hall.
She uses AI **now and then**, adopting tools after they prove useful on actual site problems.
Her **four-month buffer** and Dalia’s care wages cover short gaps, but not years without work.
She seeks **paid practice**, union evidence on hours and real vacancies before considering fewer shifts.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** leaves only about three years before robots could take fitting work and outlast their savings.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **paid supervised practice**, honest staffing dates and clear displacement support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew the measuring app is useful for a second look, but the real mark is still on the timber. I would be glad if our contractor stopped calling every new screen a revolution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I would welcome a stable pace because I still need practice on stair trim and handrails. My partner Dalia and I have around four months of expenses saved, yet a long pause between sites could eat through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking my paid shifts at the community hall rebuild and use the app only to check measurements I have already made. In the first year I would keep the Saturday repair sessions with the senior carpenter and ask about the next site before the hall closes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel fairly calm while the hall work lasts and a little tense about what comes after. I am not looking for a grand rescue from a tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the Saturday sessions cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The senior carpenter shows me how to scribe trim against walls that are nowhere near straight. I left school early and changed into this work late, so hands-on correction is worth more to me than another tutorial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you build that cash buffer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dalia does paid care visits, and we set money aside when both of us had full weeks. Our children are grown and pay their own way, which gave us room to build the buffer.

say: I would say **measuring apps** are useful as a second check.
I would ask the contractor to stop calling each **new screen** a revolution.
think: I welcome **time to practise** stair trim and handrails.
Our **four-month buffer** would shrink during a long gap between sites.
do: Keep taking **hall rebuild** shifts and checking marked measurements.
Attend **Saturday repair sessions** and ask about the next site early.
feel: **Mostly calm** during the contract, with some worry about its end.
S0.quote: I am not looking for a grand rescue from a tool.
fieldNote: Vera uses AI **occasionally** for measurement checks, while her main learning comes from supervised work with a carpenter.
The household has a **moderate reserve** from full working weeks, but a prolonged contract gap would erode it.

steps.text: Keep taking paid community hall rebuild shifts
Attend Saturday repair sessions and ask about the next site

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say faster ordering could save trips to the yard, but it should not turn every crew member into an unpaid checker of the office system. I would ask the union steward to see the new job times before they reach the rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know the hall supervisor could use AI to price and schedule every small repair, then expect me to work at the speed of a senior carpenter. My skill is still below theirs, so I could lose shifts if the new numbers hide the awkward corners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the supervisor to show me the AI order checker after it has worked on two deliveries. In the first year I would keep my paid fitting shifts and bring my record of difficult handrail jobs to a union meeting about the new targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel curious about a proven tool and annoyed at the possibility of doing extra work for free. A saved yard trip should buy time for a proper fit, not a shorter shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait for two deliveries?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One clean delivery could be luck; I want to see whether the checker catches the wrong brackets when it matters. If it does, I can learn it with a colleague beside me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the union to ask?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask that the times include measuring and fixing a crooked stair, not only attaching a straight piece. I would show the steward the notes from last Thursday’s handrail.

say: I would say **faster ordering** should save travel time, not create unpaid checking.
I would ask for **job times** to be shown before they reach the rota.
think: I fear **senior-worker targets** could cost me shifts as a learner.
I suspect **awkward corners** will disappear from the office numbers.
do: Learn the **AI order checker** after two useful delivery trials.
Keep taking **paid fitting shifts** during the first year.
Bring **handrail records** to the union meeting about targets.
feel: **Curious** about proven tools, annoyed by possible unpaid work.
S1.quote: A saved yard trip should buy time for a proper fit, not a shorter shift.
fieldNote: Vera is open to AI after **two concrete trials**, a measured form of adaptability rather than immediate adoption.
She wants the **union record** to include difficult work that a simple completion count would miss.

steps.text: Learn the AI order checker after two useful delivery trials
Keep taking paid handrail fitting shifts
Bring documented difficult jobs to the union target meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the 2028 system can draw and order the whole hall, but people still have to work in its crooked rooms until robots can do that around 2031. I would want workers to test every machine before anyone loses a paid shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 60 in 2028, the planning team could be smaller and our work could be timed more tightly, though hands still fit rails. At 63 in 2031, robots that handle tools could take the fitting itself, and four months of savings will not carry us to retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid hall shifts now and ask the senior carpenter for signed examples of the stairs I helped repair. In 2029 I would apply for a paid maintenance post at the leisure centre while still taking site work; after the robots arrive I would ask the union office about displacement pay and funded training if my job ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel shaken and very busy. A reserve buys time to choose, but it does not make another employer appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the leisure centre post be safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I cannot know whether the centre would keep maintenance workers once robots can use tools; I would apply because it is a real wage in 2029. I would not tell anyone it was a permanent escape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dalia that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner Dalia that the hall work still pays this week and we should list the bills before touching savings. She would want dates and figures, not a speech from me about being brave.

say: I would say **thinking AI** reaches plans before robots fit crooked rooms.
I would insist on **worker testing** before paid shifts are removed.
think: At **60**, faster planning could tighten my workday even before robots.
At **63**, capable robots could replace fitting work and outrun our savings.
do: Keep **paid hall shifts** and collect signed examples of stair repairs.
Apply for **leisure centre maintenance** in 2029 while employed.
Ask the **union office** about displacement pay if robots end my job.
feel: **Shaken**, but active because the reserve only buys limited time.
S2.quote: A reserve buys time to choose, but it does not make another employer appear.
fieldNote: Vera distinguishes **2028 planning pressure** from the direct threat of 2031 robots to her tool work.
Her application is for **near-term wages**, and she explicitly doubts that leisure maintenance is robot-proof.

steps.text: Keep taking paid community hall shifts through 2029
Apply for paid leisure centre maintenance in 2029
Ask the union office about displacement pay if robots end her job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew a five-year warning should come with paid practice, not a pile of links to courses. I would ask the employer and union to agree what skills and hours the new jobs actually need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when thinking AI arrives in 2031, and it might check measurements better than I do while I still fit things by hand. By 2034 I would be 66, and robots could do the fitting too; I cannot assume our retirement money is enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would practise the AI-assisted digital layout table with the senior carpenter once it is tested on a real stair. In 2032 I would keep paid site shifts and apply for a council repairs opening; I would also enroll in a funded advanced joinery class if it includes supervised work and fits around my shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel more hopeful because I have time to learn carefully. I would still worry that the class could improve me just as the job itself disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why advanced joinery when you are still learning basics?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I call it advanced because it covers stair shapes beyond the basic straight cuts I can manage now. I would need the senior carpenter’s help there; a certificate alone would not make me quick or safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you decline the class?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would decline if the fee came from our rent buffer or if attendance meant losing more wages than we could replace. Funded practice on a real staircase would be worth trying.

say: I would ask for **paid practice** matched to actual jobs.
I would want **employer and union** agreement on the hours new skills require.
think: At **63**, thinking AI may outcheck my measurements while I still fit rails.
At **66**, robots could fit rails before our retirement income is secure.
do: Practise the **digital layout table** after a real-stair trial.
Apply for **council repairs** in 2032 while keeping site shifts.
Enroll in **funded joinery class** if supervised and compatible with paid work.
feel: **Hopeful** about learning time, worried the job may vanish anyway.
S3.quote: I would still worry that the class could improve me just as the job itself disappears.
fieldNote: Vera seeks **tested equipment** and supervised joinery rather than a certificate without practical work.
She protects the **rent buffer** by making training conditional on funding and continued paid shifts.

steps.text: Practise the AI-assisted digital layout table after a real-stair trial
Keep taking paid site shifts in 2032
Apply for a council repairs opening in 2032
Enroll in funded supervised joinery if attendance preserves paid work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say ten years gives older learners a fair chance to finish training and work, if employers keep us on the rota. I would ask the union to track whether new equipment actually leaves enough paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 in 2036, my knees might already limit ladders, even before thinking AI handles the checks. At 71 in 2039, robots could do the remaining fitting; our savings are a bridge, not a wage for the rest of life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking the lower-ladder site jobs I can do safely and add to savings after full-pay months. In 2037 I would review Dalia’s care income and our actual bills, apply for a part-time paid fittings role at the housing cooperative if it is posted, and decide on fewer shifts only when the numbers work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel patient, but not complacent. Ten years gives me room to work, and it also gives employers room to quietly stop calling older workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you expect your grown children to fill a gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children have their own homes, and I would not put their wages in our retirement calculation. I would ask them for practical help in a crisis, but we should pay our own bills if we can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the union track lost hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring my rota and wage slips to the union branch each quarter so it could compare promised hours with paid hours. A story about training is less useful than seeing who still gets paid.

say: I would ask for **older learners** to stay on paid rotas.
I would ask the union to track **actual paid hours** after equipment changes.
think: At **68**, my knees may limit ladder work before thinking AI arrives.
At **71**, robots could end fitting work while savings remain only a bridge.
do: Keep **safe site shifts** and add to savings after full-pay months.
Bring **rotas and wage slips** to the union branch quarterly.
Apply for **cooperative fittings** work in 2037 if a paid opening appears.
feel: **Patient**, while alert to quiet losses of older workers’ hours.
S4.quote: A story about training is less useful than seeing who still gets paid.
fieldNote: Vera uses the long warning to track **real paid hours**, not merely employer promises of training.
Her decision to reduce shifts depends on **actual household income**, while grown children remain outside the budget.

steps.text: Keep taking safe paid site shifts in 2037
Add to household savings after full-pay months
Bring rotas and wage slips to the union branch quarterly
Apply for paid housing cooperative fittings work if posted
